etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Wasei eigo (和製英語; pseudo-anglicism), derived from cunning.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English jumper.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English bestseller.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 下(した) (shita-, “preliminary”) + 調(しら)べ (shirabe, “investigating”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 調(しら)べる (shiraberu, “to investigate”))

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 交ふ (mazifu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 他動 (tadō, “other-moving, other-acting”) + 詞 (shi, “word; part of speech”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Chinese 圓滿 /圆满 (yuánmǎn), calque of Sanskrit परिपूर्ण (paripūrṇa).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 切(せつ) (setsu, “urgent, pressing, close”) + ない (-nai, adjectivizing suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Doublet of 増さる (masaru, “to increase”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 化 (ka, “to change into”) + 石 (seki, “stone”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 及(およ)ぶ (oyobu, “to reach”).
Compare Middle Korean 및 (mìch) / Korean 및 (mit) from Middle Korean 및다〮 (mìchtá).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The quadrigrade conjugation pattern (modern quintigrade) is a result from an irregular shift from the earlier bigrade pattern, with the expected modern form being this terms doublet of 合わせる (awaseru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 飽く気なし (aku ke nashi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/moko/ → *⟨muko₁⟩ → */mukʷo/*⟨mo₍₁₎ko₁⟩ → */mʷokʷo/ → /muko/
Found in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the ideographic spelling 聟.
Although the reading muko is not confirmed in Old Japanese documents, the presence of cognate words suggests that this may be from Proto-Japonic *moko (cognate with Okinawan 婿 (mūku), Kunigami 婿 (mufu), Miyako 婿 (muku) and the moko below). This would be the a result of a phonological change, whereby non-final */o/ in Proto-Japonic nouns shifted to become /u/ in Central Old Japanese.
In regard to the derivation, there are some theories proposed, however many of them are associated with the verbs 向かう (mukau, “to go towards”) and 迎える (mukaeru, “to receive”), both derived from 向く (muku, “to turn toward”), from Proto-Japonic *muk-, from the idea of "the facing party, the other person (of a pair)"; see also 向こう (mukō, “the other side, the facing side”). Theories to explain this inconsistency in the proto-forms have not been published yet.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/moko/ → ⟨mo₍₁₎ko₁⟩ → */mʷokʷo/ → /moko/
From other Old Japanese dialects besides Central Old Japanese, with a conserved */o/ as ⟨o₁⟩.
Possibly cognate or otherwise related with Old Japanese もこ (mo₁ko₁, “companion, fellow”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 婿 (MC sejH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 孤兒 (MC ku nye|ngej).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mi₂nasigo₁⟩ → */mɨnasiᵑɡo/ → /minaɕiɡo/
身(み) (mi, “identity, family”) + 無(な)し (nashi, “none, without”) + 子(こ) (ko, “child”).
The ko changes to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
The spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).
First attested in Shōsōin documents from 702 in the name 巳奈志児刀良売 (mi₂nasigo₁-to₁ra-me₁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 馴(な)れ付(つ)く (naretsuku, literally “to be attached intimately”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 所在 (MC srjoX dzojH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 持(も)ち切(き)る (mochikiru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 日 (hi, “sun”) + の (no, attributive particle) + 丸 (maru, “circle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with 盛る (sakaru, “to become frisky, to flourish”) and 栄す, 盛す (sakasu, “to make something lively”), ultimately deriving from 咲く (saku, “to bloom”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Probably coined in Japan from Middle Chinese-derived components, as a compound of 汽 (ki, “steam”) + 船 (sen, “boat, ship”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Semantic shift from 曝(しゃ)れる (shareru), itself a phonetic shift from 曝(さ)れる (sareru).
Alternatively, derived from the classical lower bigrade conjugation verb 戯(さ)る (saru), from which 戯(ざ)れる (zareru) is also derived.
First cited to a text from 1660.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.
Originally from the 已然形 (izenkei, “realis form”) of verb 張る (haru, “to become taut or tense”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of 己 (ono, “oneself”) + つ (tsu, possessive particle) + 柄 (kara, “quality, characteristic”, later developing senses of “from, because”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appeared in 英和対訳袖珍辞書 (“A Pocket Dictionary of the English and Japanese Language”) of 1862.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *napay.
Apophonic form of 苗(なわ) (nawa, “seedling”, bound form, only used in compounds), similar to nouns such as 神 (kami, kan-, kamu-, “god”) and 目 (me, ma-, “eye”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Perhaps from 親 (oya, “parent”) + 父 (chichi, “father”). The reading appears to be an alteration of an earlier form, oyachichi, perhaps under the influence of 爺 (chichi, jiji, jī, “old man”). The kanji are jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Chinese 親父 /亲父 (qīnfù).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 観 (kan, “to view”) + 点 (ten, “point”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 過(あやま)つ (ayamatsu, “to err, make a mistake”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/daudiau/ → /dɔːd͡ʑɔː/ → /doːʑoː/
From Middle Chinese 道場 (MC dawX drjang, literally “way + place”), itself originally a translation of Sanskrit बोधिमण्ड (bodhimaṇḍa, “seat of wisdom”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 鳥 (tori, “bird”) + 居 (i, “abode”). From old legends about birds possessed by kami and sitting on tree branches.
First cited to a text from 922 CE.
